cards.text: Jerusalem has fallen, and God's people have been carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 25:8-11). This psalm is their song from far away. It opens by the rivers of Babylon, where they sit and remember Zion.

cards.question: By the rivers of Babylon, God's people remember Zion. What do they do there?

cards.text: There on the willows, they hang up their harps. I know that feeling, friend: in the junk drawer I went YEARS without one single joke, and now look at me, I can't STOP.

cards.question: The captives hang their harps on the willows in Babylon. What was going on there?

answers.text: Their captors demanded songs of joy
Their harps had all broken strings
Their leaders told them to stay silent

cards.question: The captors don't want just any song. They want the captives to sing a song about Babylon.

cards.text: Picture your boss catching you on your worst day: "Come on, SMILE! Tell everybody something FUN!" Then the psalm asks a question of its own.

cards.question: The captives are far from Zion, in Babylon. The psalm asks, "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a ___ land?"

cards.text: Now the "we" turns into "I." The singer speaks straight to Jerusalem, like the city could hear every word.

cards.question: Far away in Babylon, the singer makes a solemn promise to Jerusalem. What is it?

answers.text: To return to it before dying

cards.question: If the singer ever forgets Jerusalem, the singer asks for a right hand that stops working and a tongue stuck to the roof of the mouth.
The singer vows to exalt Jerusalem as the singer's greatest ___.

cards.text: A hand for the harp. A tongue for the song. I think the singer is betting every last note on Jerusalem.
Then the singer turns to the LORD and brings up the sons of Edom, the people who came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). It goes back to the day Jerusalem fell.

cards.question: On the day Jerusalem fell, what were the sons of Edom saying about the city?

answers.text: Tear it down to its foundations

cards.question: The singer asks the LORD to forget what the sons of Edom said the day Jerusalem fell.

cards.text: There's that word again: remember. Now the singer turns to Babylon itself: "O Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction"

cards.question: The singer wants Babylon repaid. In what way?

answers.text: As Babylon has done to them
With silver and gold for their losses
With a long exile of its own

cards.question: The singer says the one who repays Babylon as Babylon has done to them is ___.

cards.text: Then comes the last line, and it's the hardest one in the psalm: "Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks." That's where the psalm ends, friend, and it doesn't tidy anything up.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 7 quotes "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a ___ land?", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: "This psalm is their song from far away" says the psalm was sung in exile. The text never says where the singer is. It looks back in the past tense ("we sat and wept," "we hung our harps"), so the singer's location when singing should stay open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "I know that feeling" states as fact that the captives felt what Papa Dorin felt when he gave up and stopped joking. That is a feeling the text never gives, and it isn't marked as his guess. The text links the hung harps to the captors' demand (v. 3, "for"), not to despair.

rule.text: Feelings: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: The question says "far from Zion, in Babylon," which hands the baker "foreign" and rules out "promised." Only "peaceful" is left as a real option.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "Far away in Babylon, the singer makes a solemn promise" places the vow in Babylon. Verses 5-6 don't say where the singer is, and verses 1-3 look back in the past tense.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question keeps "exalt" and "greatest," and the wrong answers are "fear" and "burden." Nobody exalts something as their greatest fear or burden, so "joy" stands out. "Joy" was also already shown in card 4's answer ("songs of joy").

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: This card recaps verses 5-6, which cards 9-11 already covered, and moves nothing forward. "A hand for the harp. A tongue for the song." is also stated as fact, but the text never connects the right hand to the harp or the tongue to the song.
"A hand for the harp. A tongue for the song." connects the vow in verses 5-6 to harp-playing and singing. The text doesn't make that connection.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "There's that word again: remember" points to "Remember" in verse 7, but the card only cites Psalm 137:8. It should cite Psalm 137:7-8.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: "The singer wants Babylon repaid" gives away card 18. If the singer wants the repayment, the repayer is viewed well, which rules out "cursed" and "foolish." Also, the text doesn't say the singer "wants" anything. It pronounces the repayer blessed.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: "The singer wants Babylon repaid" calls the line something the text doesn't. Verse 8 says "blessed is he who repays you"; it pronounces a blessing and never says what the singer wants.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "With a long exile of its own" is close to the right answer, "As Babylon has done to them." Babylon carried the captives into exile, so a baker could argue that repaying Babylon as it has done means an exile of its own.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The wrong answers "cursed" and "foolish" don't fit after card 17 establishes that the singer wants Babylon repaid, so "blessed" stands out as the only positive word.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.
